curatedSummaries.legalOrStandardInstrument: SFRS(I) 9 §4.1.1-§4.1.5 Financial Assets - Business Model and Contractual Cash Flow Classification
curatedSummaries.documentTitle: Financial Assets - Business Model and Contractual Cash Flow Classification
curatedSummaries.sourceText: A financial asset is classified using both the entity’s business model for managing the asset and the asset’s contractual cash flow characteristics. A debt asset is measured at amortised cost when it is held within a business model whose objective is to collect contractual cash flows and its contractual terms give rise on specified dates to cash flows that are solely payments of principal and interest on the principal amount outstanding. A qualifying debt asset held in a business model achieved by both collecting contractual cash flows and selling is measured at fair value through other comprehensive income. Assets outside those categories are measured at fair value through profit or loss, subject to the applicable designation and scope requirements.
curatedSummaries.principleSummary: Financial Assets - Business Model and Contractual Cash Flow Classification

curatedSummaries.legalOrStandardInstrument: SFRS(I) 1-20 §7, §12, §24 & §29 Accounting for Government Grants and Disclosure of Government Assistance
curatedSummaries.documentTitle: Accounting for Government Grants and Disclosure of Government Assistance
curatedSummaries.sourceText: Government grants shall not be recognized until there is reasonable assurance that the entity will comply with conditions attaching to them and the grants will be received (§7). Grants shall be recognized in profit or loss on a systematic basis over the periods in which the entity recognizes as expenses the related costs which the grants are intended to compensate (§12). Capital grants related to assets may be presented either as deferred income or by deducting the grant in arriving at the carrying amount of the asset (§24). Operating grants (e.g. wage credits, hiring incentives) may be presented as other income or deducted from the related expense (§29).
curatedSummaries.principleSummary: Accounting for Government Grants and Disclosure of Government Assistance

curatedSummaries.documentTitle: Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors
curatedSummaries.sourceText: An entity shall change an accounting policy only if the change is required by an SFRS(I) or results in more reliable and relevant information (§14). Changes in accounting policy are accounted for retrospectively (§19). The effect of a change in an accounting estimate (e.g. useful life, residual value, bad debt allowance percentage) shall be recognized prospectively by including it in profit or loss in the period of change and future periods (§32). Material prior period errors must be corrected retrospectively in the first set of financial statements authorised for issue after their discovery by restating comparative amounts (§42).
curatedSummaries.principleSummary: Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors

curatedSummaries.legalOrStandardInstrument: SFRS(I) 9 §4.1.4, §5.7.5-§5.7.6 & B5.7.1 Classification of Equity Instruments
curatedSummaries.sourceText: An investment in an equity instrument is measured at fair value through profit or loss unless the entity makes the irrevocable election at initial recognition to present subsequent changes in fair value in other comprehensive income for an investment that is neither held for trading nor contingent consideration recognised by an acquirer in a business combination within IFRS 3. Amounts accumulated in OCI for an elected investment are not subsequently reclassified to profit or loss on disposal; a transfer within equity may be made.

finalResponse.messageText:
# Direct Answer

Accrual accounting and cash accounting represent two different methods of recording business transactions, which significantly impacts how unpaid supplier invoices are treated in a small business's financial statements.

# Explanation

- Under accrual accounting, transactions are recognized when they occur rather than when cash changes hands.
- For a small business with unpaid supplier invoices, this means expenses and corresponding liabilities (accounts payable) are recorded when the goods or services are received or when the obligation is incurred, regardless of when payment is eventually made.
- Under cash accounting, revenues and expenses are recognized strictly when cash is received or paid.
- For unpaid supplier invoices, a cash-basis business does not record an expense or a liability when the invoice is received; the transaction remains unrecorded in the financial records until the cash payment is actually disbursed to the supplier.
- The choice between these two methods changes the timing and appearance of business performance.
- Accrual accounting provides a comprehensive view of current obligations and upcoming cash outflows by capturing outstanding bills, whereas cash accounting offers a simpler view focused strictly on historical cash movements.

# Accounting Treatment

- Recognition of an expense and a payable under accrual accounting depends on the underlying transaction, such as the delivery of goods or performance of services, rather than the presence of an invoice or the timing of cash settlement.
- Entity-specific capitalization policies, materiality thresholds, and the applicable financial reporting framework must be verified to determine whether a given supplier purchase should be recognized immediately as an expense or capitalized as an asset.

# Conditions and Important Notes

- The applicable financial reporting framework and legal reporting requirements for the specific entity must be checked to determine which accounting basis is permitted or required.

# Verification Note

A specific rate, deadline, calculation, legal requirement, or provision reference is not included because this answer path has not independently verified that claim.
